extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and historians of mathematics interested in G. H. Hardy
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic biography of the mathematician G. H. Hardy covering his life, career, mathematical work, personality, and cultural impact. Useful for readers seeking factual and interpretive information about Hardy and his contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy is credited with reforming British mathematics by bringing rigour into it, promoting the more precise continental 'cours d'analyse' methods over the older Cambridge Tripos/applied tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Hardy's advocacy for rigorous, precise methods (e.g., cours d'analyse), his opposition to Tripos as an end in itself, and his role in shifting British mathematics toward rigorous pure analysis and analytic number theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuing pure mathematics for aesthetic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy preferred pure mathematics and judged mathematical work by aesthetic and 'permanent' value rather than immediate usefulness; he famously claimed that mathematicians 'glory in the uselessness' insofar as remoteness preserves gentleness and cleanliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy's Apology is cited to show his view that 'real' mathematics has permanent aesthetic value; he rejected utility as the primary criterion and considered independence from the physical world and enduring beauty as marks of high-quality mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of practical utility as primary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy asserted that lack of practical application does not diminish the value of mathematical work and explicitly distanced his own work from 'useful' applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page quotes Hardy's lines ('I have never done anything "useful"') and explains his belief that the best mathematics may be remote from ordinary human activities; while noting some of his work later found applications, this skepticism is presented as an evaluative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for methods aligned with continental analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy recommended and worked within the precise traditions of continental analysis (e.g., influenced by Camille Jordan's Cours d'analyse), favoring those methods as superior to the older Cambridge applied tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: Hardy's independent study of continental texts shaped his conception of what mathematics 'really meant' and guided his research and teaching choices; this functions as an implicit methodological standard in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration effectiveness and complementary roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy–Littlewood collaboration is presented as a model of a highly successful mathematical partnership, where complementary strengths (ideas vs. detailed execution) produced major advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts Hardy's remarks about Littlewood contributing ideas while Hardy handled the 'tedious part', and highlights their joint achievements (e.g., circle method, conjectures) as evidence that productive collaborations with clear complementary roles are a virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and mentorship of exceptional talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's prompt recognition and mentoring of Ramanujan is presented as a key achievement, implying the importance of identifying and fostering extraordinary mathematical talent even when untutored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Hardy's initial skepticism of Ramanujan's letter followed by rapid recognition of its genuineness and subsequent mentorship; this narrative implies criteria for good mentorship: discernment, willingness to support unconventional talent, and collaborative engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic and institutional contributions as markers of esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Positions, honors, and published collected papers are used in the article to indicate Hardy's standing and the quality of his contributions (e.g., Prize Fellowship, Savilian Chair, Royal/Copley Medals, collected papers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biography lists offices held, awards received, election to academies, and collected papers—presenting institutional recognition and publication record as signals of a mathematician's impact and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical clarity and lecture preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy's lecturing style (carefully prepared, lucid, with intellectually satisfying denouements) is highlighted as exemplary teaching practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freeman Dyson's recollection of Hardy's lectures emphasizes precision, lucidity, careful preparation, and the intellectual payoff near the end of the lecture—offering an implicit standard for effective mathematical exposition and teaching.
